title: This week's cases
sub: Fake refunds, fee scares and the hotlines to save

msg.text: You have excess CPF contributions of $1,284.60 to be refunded. Verify your bank details within 48 hours: cpf-refund-sg.com/claim

ex.why: In Aug 2026 the CPF Board warned about phishing emails promising refunds of 'excess' contributions. Fake government refunds are a common trick in every country. Agencies don't ask you to confirm bank details through an email link, so check in the official app or website instead.

ex.q: Tap every red flag in this call

segs.text: Hello, I'm calling about your insurance policy.
A new policy fee of $499 will be deducted automatically tonight.
To cancel, I'll transfer you to a bank officer now.
Please install this app so we can help you cancel.

ex.why: Singapore police named 'insurance services' scams as a new type. A caller warns that a fee is about to be charged, then hands you to a fake bank or police officer. Hang up and call your insurer on the number in your policy or their official app.

source.label: Dollars and Sense: new scam types in Singapore

ex.q: In 2026 the UK replaced Action Fraud with a new national service. What is it called?
ex.why: Report Fraud, run by the City of London Police, is where people in England, Wales and Northern Ireland now report fraud and cybercrime, at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040.

source.label: techUK: Report Fraud replaces Action Fraud

ex.q: In Malaysia, what happens when you call the 997 scam hotline?
opts: It runs 24 hours and your call counts as a police report
ex.why: Since September 2025 the National Scam Response Centre's 997 line has run around the clock, and calls are treated as police reports, so banks can move faster to freeze money.

ex.q: Match each country to its scam hotline
ex.why: Save your country's number before you need it. The Report tab always shows yours.
